paper_title: Efficient Ensemble for Fine-tuning Language Models on Multiple Datasets
caption: We show the empirical generalization errors (termed Error in the figures) and estimated Hessian traces of the loss for fine-tuned adapters (using QAdapter on Llama-3-8B) across various hidden dimensions. Smaller adapters achieve the lowest generalization errors. Additionally, the Hessian trace values correlate with generalization errors, suggesting that smaller adapters tend to converge to flatter minima.
model_annotation: The diagram displays empirical generalization errors, termed “Errors (COPA)”, plotted against the rank of adapter sizes, which corresponds to different hidden dimensions used in fine-tuned adapters based on the QAdapter method applied to the Llama-3-8B model. The x-axis, labeled “Rank”, uses a linear scale with tick marks at the values 4, 16, 64, and 256, representing the adapter sizes in descending order of dimensionality, and is unlabeled in terms of units. The y-axis, labeled “Errors (COPA)”, uses a linear scale ranging from 0.0 to 0.6, with tick marks at 0.0, 0.3, and 0.6, and represents the magnitude of generalization error. A single solid black line connects four data points, each marked with a solid green circle, indicating the error values at each rank: at rank 4, the error is approximately 0.22; at rank 16, the error is approximately 0.18; at rank 64, the error rises to approximately 0.38; and at rank 256, the error stabilizes at approximately 0.39. The error bars, extending vertically from each data point, indicate the estimated uncertainty or variability in the error measurements.

model_annotations.English: This line plot illustrates empirical generalization errors, labeled as “Errors (COPA)”, across different adapter ranks. The x-axis, labeled “Rank”, uses a linear scale ranging from 4 to 256, with tick labels spaced at intervals of 12 (4, 16, 64, 256). The y-axis, labeled “Errors (COPA)”, uses a linear scale ranging from 0.0 to 0.6. A single black line with solid style connects circular green markers at each rank point. The error value starts at approximately 0.22 at rank 4, decreases slightly to approximately 0.20 at rank 16, then increases sharply to approximately 0.38 at rank 64, and remains relatively stable at approximately 0.38 at rank 256. Vertical error bars are present at each data point, indicating uncertainty in the measured error values.
